b: Ngozi Onwurah’s Welcome II the Terrordome, which the record books now dispassionately file away as the first theatrically distributed British feature directed by a Black woman, refuses to bend to meet its audience in the middle. It’s an unrelenting howl, and more than three decades later, it feels like the world is still just catching up.

The setup is blunt and the action simple. In a near future, Black people have been segregated into a slum called the Terrordome, named for the incendiary Public Enemy single, where violence threatens to boil over after a young Black boy’s murder. The boy’s mother, Angela (Suzette Llewellyn), resolutely and almost calmly answers her son’s killing with a vengeful rampage.

Meanwhile, Angela’s neighbor Jodie (Saffron Burrows), a white woman pregnant by her Black boyfriend, Spike (Valentine Nonyela), pays a harsh price when both communities disapprove of their domestic situation. (Spike Lee had just dissected the guardrails preventing interracial love from flourishing in his 1991 film Jungle Fever, and that a key character here shares his name is surely no accident.) As in Lee’s films, the soundtrack both comments on and drives the action. Onwurah has said that every event in Welcome II the Terrordome is based on something that really happened, compressed into a single night so audiences couldn’t let the headlines blur.

Contemporary British critics were, cough, not amused. Paul Gilroy, writing in Sight and Sound, called the film “fascist,” and detractors more broadly found it too violent and hopeless, a nihilistic howl without solutions. A howl of rage with no instruction manual is, last I checked, exactly what rage is, and it’s to the film’s credit that it deliberately polarizes and never apologizes. Onwurah has said that reactions varied depending on the room, that Black-only screenings drew a completely different response than press screenings, and that critics kept pressing her to supply a palatable solution she declined to invent. As she put it, one doesn’t need to bring a solution to the table to be justified in one’s anger.

In the same Sight and Sound takedown, Gilroy dismissed the film as “artistically and conceptually inept,” and even its more sympathetic scholars concede the continuity problems and budgetary restrictions. But the dramatics, the poetics (first and foremost those folkloric bookends), and the patchy craftsmanship all seem to lean into opposition to the canonical idea of “quality” filmmaking, in the spirit of Oscar Micheaux, whose roughness was derided for decades before critics insisted that his shortcomings were, in their own way, pedagogically useful. Whether you call the results inept or inspired may say less about the film than about what you’ve been trained to think a Black filmmaker’s rage is allowed to look like.

Still, be warned that the film asks a lot of its audience. Surrendering to Welcome II the Terrordome means accepting its didacticism, a pan-Africanist education that works fragments of Malcolm X’s speeches into the script, as well as the idiosyncratic dead ends that tend to survive in low-budget productions with less editorial oversight. Your patience may be tested by the scenes of would-be revolutionaries running kung fu drills in their dojo, especially since they promise a collective uprising that never really materializes. Micheaux, whose films were never shy about uplift, would have understood. You either take the lectures and the detours as the price of admission or you don’t, and the film isn’t waiting for you to make up your mind.

What gets somewhat lost in the enthusiasm of rediscovery is that Welcome II the Terrordome is the work of a biracial filmmaker whose other films point to a grim ambivalence about her lineage. Onwurah was born in Nigeria to a Nigerian father and a white British mother, and raised in a predominantly white English community. Her 1988 short “Coffee Coloured Children,” which is included as an extra on this Blu-ray, follows two mixed-race kids who scour their skin with powder in a desperate attempt to look white.

Which makes it all the more striking what Welcome II the Terrordome does with that same pain. A few years before Warren Beatty’s Bulworth had its white senator rap that the “cure” for racism is for everybody to keep fucking until we’re all the same color, Onwurah, who knows a thing or two about being the supposed solution, had already refused that glib premise. Jodie, who Onwurah told Reverse Shot is loosely based on her own white mother, bears the film’s most pointed rebuttal: The child she carries, meant to be a bridge, is lost to the violence around her, and she’s left too white for one side and not white enough for the other.

The film isn’t a tract, and Jodie is among its most sympathetic figures, but the message is hard to miss. Coexistence in its most directly biological form, miscegenation, is no refuge from a world that has already decided who’s disposable. That message is at its most spiritual in the film’s bold bookends, the sequences that Gilroy, among others, waved away as a sop to Black audiences’ emotions. The opening dramatizes the legend of the 1803 Igbo Landing, in which enslaved Africans are said to have walked into the water rather than live in bondage.

Onwurah has described Welcome II the Terrordome as her attempt to answer what happened to those who went under. Did they die, return to the ancestors, or end up in an in-between zone that she calls the Terrordome? The film’s moral logic is that there’s more nobility in rejecting any existence on white people’s terms, even to the point of death, than in negotiating a synthesis with them. When the film finally sails home, with its characters setting foot on the “land of the ancestors” and crusader Black Rad (Felix Joseph) declaring that it’s time for “war with our enemies and peace with our spirits,” the anger and the grief turn out to be the same thing.

Onwurah’s argument is that the institutions guarding the Terrordome’s gates can’t be reasoned with, because they were built precisely to produce the Terrordome. The film’s uprising doesn’t petition the police or the press. Black Rad’s complaint that he’s “sick of going to funerals” wouldn’t be out of place at any protest of the last decade. In the ’90s, that read as gloomy nihilism. Now that many governments have at least begun to say out loud what the film’s bookends insist on, that there’s no polishing the history of chattel slavery, it reads closer to a clear-eyed account of what refusal looks like once negotiation has been tried and found to be a trap. If Welcome II the Terrordome is right, and I’d argue it is, there’s no choice but to reject the institutions built to get us here, up to and including cinematic traditions of quality.

To that end, it’s worth noting that Welcome II the Terrordome’s transfer is probably among the least traditionally “demo-worthy” of any Criterion disc since The Signifyin’ Works of Marlon Riggs, another major stake in the ground for Black filmmakers’ visibility from an era that underfunded and deprioritized Black stories, lives, and cinema. Criterion presents the film in its original 1.37:1 aspect ratio from a new 2K digital restoration supervised and approved by cinematographer Alwin H. Küchler. Onwurah has said that she specifically wanted a “filmic aesthetic,” shooting on film and taking care to light Black skin properly, in reaction to the way low-budget Black films were expected to look “urban” and “gritty.”

The restoration preserves the dark, menacing slums of the Terrordome, but also, it must be said, a cloudiness and middling contrast that keep the image from ever registering the richness of skin tone. Whether that’s down to the surviving elements or the restoration is up for grabs, but where Riggs’s video-born imperfections read as part of the work, the murk here somewhat works against a film that so badly wanted to look like cinema. The 2.0 surround DTS-HD Master Audio soundtrack fares considerably better. Dialogue is clear, and the bass on the music is booming and full, befitting a film named after arguably Public Enemy’s brashest moment.

Criterion’s supplements are as generous as they are essential. The audio commentary, featuring Küchler, Onwurah, and moderator Ashley Clark, is a must-listen, rich with production history and cogent critical analysis from Clark. In a new interview, Onwurah is in a touchingly ambivalent place about the film’s history and how long it took the world to catch up to it. She also speaks at length about her complicated relationship to her racial identity, including having to tip her mother off about an early film’s very pointed look at whiteness.

As if that weren’t enough, three of Onwurah’s short films are included. Both the aforementioned “Coffee Coloured Children” and 2001’s “Hang Time,” a remix of the Robert Johnson legend, are well worth taking in, but the most compelling is 1993’s “And Still I Rise,” an unabashedly intersectional feminist documentary short on Black women’s sexuality and the need to reclaim authorship of their own lives and experiences. Finally, there’s a fantastic booklet essay by Kadish Morris that puts the film in its proper (furious) context.
Thirty years on, the world is catching up to what Ngozi Onwurah’s film refused to gloss over, and Criterion’s supplements make its case with fitting force. If only the disc’s image matched.
